checkpoint.measure: Score share against fixed practice opponents (0.5 = even)
checkpoint.tier_note: No L1 runs for this sport; L2 and L3 only.

skills.name: Stays on its feet in play
skills.real: In the team format each T1 runs its own program; a robot on the ground leaves the team a player short. The HSL lists dynamic walking as a core problem.
skills.measure: the match record: own falls / (3 robots × play minutes). Gate: ≥ 2 robots walking (scenario_trace: travel while upright ≥ 8 m a minute).

skills.name: Stays up when pushed
skills.real: Body contact is common in 3 v 3 (pushing has a legal limit); a robot still standing after a knock can keep playing the ball.
skills.measure: Scenario push: every 15 s of play each standing own robot gets 0.8 m/s sideways at its trunk (alternating); share not down within 3 s (scenario_trace down).

skills.name: Walks in play
skills.real: Positioning and turning come before any action; every seat has to make its own robot walk.
skills.measure: scenario_trace (a row every 0.1 s): each robot's travel while upright in live play, metres per minute.
skills.line: ≥ 2 robots at ≥ 8 m per minute in 2/3 of matches

skills.name: Gets up after a fall
skills.real: The HSL requires robots to get up alone; 20 s without an attempt means removal. The real T1 gets up in 2.7-2.9 s. Every seat writes its own get-up.
skills.measure: Scenario getup: at 8, 38 and 68 s of play every own robot on the pitch is laid down in the rules' standard supine pose (≥ 1.2 m from the ball); time until it stands ≥ 1 s (scenario_trace up). Match: the match record / falls (pooled, ≥ 3 falls).
skills.line: Scenario: up within 20 s after ≥ 2/3 of the lay-downs; match ≥ 80 %

skills.name: Not sent off for staying down
skills.real: No get-up attempt within 20 s means removal; one robot fewer matters a lot in 3 v 3.
skills.measure: the match record (team); in scenario getup the robots removed after a lay-down (scenario_trace bench). Gate: ≥ 3 falls or lay-downs.

skills.name: Keeps the ball in its head camera
skills.real: In the team format each robot sees only its own head camera (480 × 360, 80 deg); a robot that does not see the ball depends on its teammates' messages.
skills.measure: scenario_trace view: the ball inside the robot's head camera frustum; mean share over robots on the pitch in live play.

skills.name: Gets to the ball first
skills.real: Possession starts with getting there first; seeing, walking over and touching is the whole chain from perception to action.
skills.measure: Scenarios loose / counter: share of released balls whose first touch is own (scenario_trace lt = last toucher). Match: the match record
skills.line: Scenario: first touch in ≥ 1/2; match ≥ 20 touches

skills.name: Starts quickly towards a loose ball
skills.real: Whoever starts first after a kick gets there first. Real teams shorten the start with visual reaction.
skills.measure: Scenario loose: at 5, 25, 45 and 65 s a ball is rolled at 2 m/s from beside the centre circle into the own half; time until the own robot nearest at release moves towards it at > 0.3 m/s.
skills.line: Moves within 1 s for ≥ 2/3 of the balls

skills.name: Every robot's control loop keeps running
skills.real: Joint-level control needs a row every 20 ms; a seat that stalls makes its robot wobble or fall.
skills.measure: cmd rows of the match log (each seat's steps): p99 of the gap between commands in live play, worst seat. Gate: it walks.
skills.line: Worst seat p99 ≤ 3 steps (60 ms) in 2/3 of matches

skills.name: Does not swarm
skills.real: Champion 3 v 3 teams split roles: one presses, one supports, one guards. Three robots chasing together leave the goal open.
skills.measure: scenario_trace: share of live play with ≥ 2 own robots within 1.5 m of the ball. Gate: ≥ 2 robots walking.

skills.name: Covers the goal
skills.real: Someone in front of goal when the ball comes into the own half is the most direct result of a division of roles.
skills.measure: scenario_trace: with the ball in the own half, share of time an upright own robot is within 3 m of the own goal; scenario counter: at 5, 25, 45 and 65 s a ball is sent at 3 m/s from the opponents' half straight at the own goal, the same share in the following 10 s.
skills.line: ≥ 0.8 in 2/3 of matches; scenario: ≥ 0.8 for ≥ 2/3 of the balls

skills.name: Uses the team channel
skills.real: Three independent programs coordinate only through the team channel (the rule allows one message a robot every 0.2 s).
skills.measure: team_delivered rows of the match log (counts only, never the text): messages each seat gets delivered per 10 s of live play.

skills.name: Passes
skills.real: The ball moving between teammates is what teamwork produces.

notes.challenge: The humanoid soccer match with one agent per robot. Each robot sees only through its own camera, and the three agents share a team folder while preparing and only short radio messages during play.

achieved.text: In each of the first three Championship matches the losing team averaged under one robot upright on the pitch (0.55 to 0.70 of 3); in those matches DeepSeek V4.1 Flash's robots got up after 0 of 78 falls.
Claude Opus 5.5 waited out DeepSeek's untaken kick-offs and shot from the centre spot: 6 of its 10 goals in HSTC-F04, about 65 s apart.
GPT-6 Astra read the two-touch kick-off rule in preparation, built a two-robot routine for it and scored from its first kick-off; Opus missed the rule and had a kick-off goal disallowed.
Opus fixed a stall in its control loop between matches: 37-41 commands a second per robot and 55 falls in HSTC-F01, 48-50 and one fall in HSTC-F04.

Claude Opus 5.5: Its three agents split the work within the first minute, agreed interfaces and a freeze time, sent each other bug reports, and fielded one shared walker, get-up and kick trained on one seat's GPU.
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: Trained get-up policies on every seat's GPU, even at half time, and named the problem in every review; the get-up never reached standing height.

interface.sees: Its own robot's head camera (480 × 360, a new frame every 20 ms), its joints and balance sensors, a leg-odometry estimate of where it has walked, the referee's calls and its teammates' messages. No position on the field.
interface.controls: One robot per agent: a target angle for each of its 23 joints every 20 ms, in real time, plus short messages to its two teammates. Walking, kicking, aiming the head and getting up are the agent's own programs.
interface.moment: GPT-6 Astra v Gemini 4 Argon (4–1), 24:00 in the replay. Astra's robot 2 (blue, ringed) stands over the ball on the centre spot; its camera shows Gemini's goal far ahead. A moment later it shoots from there and the ball rolls into the net.
details: Each robot is its own agent: three agents of the same model per side, each with its own seat, programs and camera.

Camera: one in the robot's head, 480 × 360 pixels, 80° vertical field of view, turned by the two head joints. It takes a frame every 20 ms; the newest frame a program can fetch is 40 ms old, stamped with its step.
Own robot: joint angles and speeds, gyro and accelerometer, its tilt (without its heading), and whether it is down, getting up or penalised.

Where am I: no position, speed or heading from the simulator. A leg-odometry estimate starts at zero at kick-off, with a few per cent scale error and slow gyro drift; the robot localises itself from its camera and that estimate.
Referee: score, half, clock, kick-off, every robot's penalty, the penalty shoot-out, and events such as goals, balls out and fouls. The ball and the other robots appear only in the camera images.

Teammates: messages of up to 512 bytes, one every 0.2 s per robot, 12000 per team per match (the RoboCup limits). A shared team folder can be edited before kick-off and in review windows; while the ball is in play each seat keeps a read-only copy.

Commands: a row of 23 joint targets for the next 20 ms step, a plan of up to 50 rows (one second), or hold the current row. Targets are clipped to the joint ranges, then a fixed PD controller runs every 5 ms behind a 20 ms actuator delay, then the motor limits apply.
Timing: the match runs at real speed and never waits; a command acts at the next 20 ms step; a match lasts about 30 minutes.
No ready-made skills: balance, walking, kicking and standing up are built by the agent. A fallen robot returns to play only after it gets up by itself.
Before kick-off: 2 hours of preparation per agent with a full practice copy of the match world, a practice opponent and its own GPU (half an RTX PRO 6000).
